1.tip: ESD hurts bare chips. Handling a bare M.2 SSD stick = ESD risk. Plugging in displays or power supplies is not.
1.why: An M.2 SSD is a bare circuit board with exposed chips, so a static spark from your hand can damage it. The other choices don't involve touching sensitive parts inside the PC.

2.tip: ESD hurts what's INSIDE the case: RAM, CPU, motherboard. Plugging in speakers or a display from outside is safe.
2.why: Electrostatic discharge can fry the tiny circuits on bare chips. When you install RAM you touch exposed memory chips and contacts, so a static spark can damage them.

3.cue: new technical job, ESD be an issue
3.tip: Bare chips in your hand = ESD danger. The CPU is the most expensive chip you'll touch.
3.why: When you install a processor you handle a bare chip with many tiny pins or pads. Static from your body can silently damage it, so you wear a wrist strap.

4.cue: new technical job, ESD be an issue
4.tip: ESD rule: open case + bare chip in hand = wear a wrist strap. RAM is a bare chip.
4.why: Static from your body can damage memory chips you handle directly. Laser printer parts are a high voltage danger to you, not an ESD danger to the PC.

5.cue: preventive maintenance, ESD be an issue
5.tip: Motherboard = the biggest bare circuit board. Biggest board, biggest ESD risk.
5.why: A motherboard is full of exposed chips and traces. Touching it without grounding yourself can send a static spark into those parts and damage them.

6.cue: assemble a PC, ESD is an issue
6.tip: Building a PC? Every bare part you snap in (RAM, CPU) needs ESD care.
6.why: Assembling a PC means installing RAM by hand, and those memory chips are easily damaged by static. Ground yourself first with a wrist strap.

7.tip: M.2 SSD is a bare stick of chips plugged into the motherboard. Bare chips = ESD risk.
7.why: An M.2 SSD has no protective case, so its memory chips are exposed while you install it on the motherboard. A static spark could damage it or the board.

8.tip: CPU pins are tiny and sensitive: ground yourself before you touch a processor.
8.why: Installing a processor means handling a bare chip and the open motherboard socket. Static from your hands could damage the CPU's delicate circuits.

9.tip: Boot = BIOS/UEFI. The firmware wakes the PC up, not the CPU or bridges.
9.why: The BIOS or its newer version, UEFI, is firmware on a motherboard chip. It tests the hardware at power on and then finds and starts the operating system.

10.cue: upgrading an ATX motherboard with another
10.tip: New board, new socket. The old CPU may not fit, so you might have to buy one.
10.why: A new motherboard may use a different CPU socket or chipset, so your old CPU may not fit or work. ATX is just the board size, so the case is fine.

11.tip: Chipset = what the board CAN do. Ports and features like eSATA come from the chipset.
11.why: The chipset controls how the CPU talks to other parts and decides which features the motherboard supports, such as eSATA, USB types and RAM speeds.

12.tip: ROM = Read Only Memory. Read only means it can't be changed.
12.why: ROM holds permanent instructions, like old boot firmware. Its contents stay when power is off and normally can't be changed, so adapter cards still use it.

13.tip: DDR = Double Data Rate: data moves twice per clock tick.
13.why: DDR moves data on both the rising and falling edge of each clock cycle, so it transfers twice as much as plain SDRAM, which uses only one edge.

14.tip: Laser printer: the corona uses HIGH VOLTAGE and the fuser is HOT. Zap and burn.
14.why: Laser printers use thousands of volts to charge the drum and a fuser that heats to about 200 C to melt toner. Unplug and let it cool before working on it.

15.cue: screws externally through the PC case
15.tip: The power supply bolts in from the BACK of the case, where its plug and fan stick out.
15.why: The power supply sits at the back of the case with its power socket outside, so you screw it in from the outside. The motherboard, CPU and RAM mount inside.

16.tip: Modern drive data cable = SATA. ATX is power, PWR_SW is the button.
16.why: Internal hard drives use a SATA data cable to the SATA port on the motherboard. ATX is the main power connector and PWR_SW is the front power button header.

17.tip: Video cards go in the long expansion slots: section D in the picture.
17.why: In the picture, section D holds the PCIe expansion slots where add-in cards like a video card go. A is power, B is SATA ports and C is the RAM slots.

18.cue: connected to the motherboard with a SATA cable
18.tip: SATA = storage: hard drives and optical (DVD) drives.
18.why: SATA cables connect drives, like hard drives and DVD optical drives, to the motherboard. Cards plug into slots and the power supply uses power cables.

19.cue: hardware failure detected by the BIOS
19.tip: POST talks in beeps. Beep codes tell you which part failed.
19.why: During POST the BIOS checks the hardware. If something fails before the screen works, it plays a beep code, a pattern of beeps that points to the bad part.

20.cue: BIOS settings to secure a computer
20.tip: BIOS security: Passwords, TPM chip, drive encryption. MAC filtering and TKIP are wireless router stuff.
20.why: In BIOS/UEFI you can set boot and setup passwords, turn on the TPM security chip and enable drive encryption. MAC filtering and TKIP are set on wireless routers.

21.tip: RAID = many drives working as a team, for safety (redundancy) or speed.
21.why: A RAID adapter links several drives so they act as one, either copying data for protection if a drive fails, or spreading data out for faster speed.

22.tip: Paste goes between the hot chip and its cooler: CPU and heat sink.
22.why: Thermal paste fills tiny air gaps between the CPU and the heat sink so heat moves well from the chip into the cooler.

23.cue: purpose of a Safety Data Sheet
23.tip: SDS = Safety Data Sheet = how to handle Dangerous Stuff.
23.why: A Safety Data Sheet explains a chemical's dangers and how to handle, store, clean up and dispose of it safely, like toner or cleaning solvents.

24.cue: cleaning the inside of a computer
24.tip: Cleaning removes dust. Dust traps heat and makes parts overheat.
24.why: Dust builds up on fans and heat sinks and blocks airflow, which makes parts run hot. Cleaning the inside removes it. EMI and ESD aren't fixed by cleaning.

25.tip: Can of air: keep it UPRIGHT, or liquid sprays out. Hold the fans still.
25.why: Tilting a can of compressed air can spray freezing liquid onto parts. Also hold fans still so they don't spin too fast, and never use window cleaner on LCDs.

26.tip: Factory with wood dust? Dust is the laptop killer: it clogs vents and fans.
26.why: Wood dust gets sucked into the laptop vents and clogs fans and heat sinks, causing overheating. The warmth and humidity are high but still within normal limits.

27.cue: testing did not identify an exact cause
27.tip: Theory failed? Make a NEW theory and WRITE DOWN what you tried.
27.why: If a test doesn't find the cause, you go back and form a new theory. Documenting each test stops you from repeating it and helps others later.

28.cue: set to 230 volts, outlet in the United States
28.tip: Too LITTLE voltage = nothing happens. Set to 230 V but fed 120 V means the PC won't start.
28.why: US outlets give about 120 V. A power supply set for 230 V gets only about half the voltage it expects, so it can't power up the PC. Too much voltage is the dangerous case.

29.tip: LAN = Local Area Network: one building or campus. WAN = wide, MAN = city, PAN = personal.
29.why: A LAN covers a small area like one building or campus, run by one organization. A WAN spans large distances and a MAN covers a city.

30.tip: Wired + fast = cable (TV coax) and DSL (phone line). Dial-up is wired but slow.
30.why: Cable Internet uses the TV coaxial cable and DSL uses phone lines, both wired and high speed. Satellite and cellular are wireless, and dial-up is very slow.

31.tip: UDP = fast and no promises. TCP = slower but guaranteed.
31.why: UDP skips the acknowledgments and ordering that TCP does, so it's faster with less overhead. Use it when speed matters more than every packet arriving, like voice or video.

32.tip: DHCP hands out IP addresses automatically. No more typing them by hand.
32.why: A DHCP server gives each workstation its IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS automatically, so you don't set them manually on every computer.

33.tip: UTM = Unified Threat Management: firewall + VPN + IDS/IPS + DoS protection in one box.
33.why: A UTM appliance combines many security features, like firewall, VPN, intrusion detection and prevention and DoS protection, in a single device. TPM is a chip in a PC.

34.tip: 169.254 = APIPA = 'I asked DHCP and nobody answered.'
34.why: When Windows can't reach a DHCP server, it gives itself an APIPA address starting with 169.254. That address only works locally, so there's no Internet.

35.tip: Basic trio: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway. (DNS helps with names, but isn't one of the three.)
35.why: The IP address identifies the PC, the subnet mask shows which addresses are local, and the default gateway is the router used to reach other networks.

36.tip: /64 = first 4 groups are network, last 4 groups are the host.
36.why: A /64 prefix means the first 64 bits (4 groups) are the network part. The last 4 groups, 0607:1234:aa10:ba01, identify the host itself.

37.tip: Apps use ports. Block the port in Windows Firewall to block the app.
37.why: Network apps listen on specific TCP or UDP ports. Blocking those ports in Windows Firewall stops traffic from reaching the app. MAC filtering is a router feature.

38.tip: Wi-Fi calling = calls over Wi-Fi when the cell signal is weak.
38.why: Wi-Fi calling routes phone calls over a Wi-Fi network instead of the cell tower, so it helps most where the cellular signal is poor, like inside some buildings.

39.tip: Laptop parts are small and custom. They don't fit desktops.
39.why: Laptop parts are built small and often proprietary, so most won't work in a desktop. Laptop boards have no standard size, and laptop CPUs do need cooling.

40.cue: bridge between laptop hardware and the operating system
40.tip: ACPI = Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: the Power Interface.
40.why: ACPI is the standard that lets the operating system control hardware power states, like sleep and hibernate, so you can set power management schemes.

41.tip: Customer can swap the easy stuff: battery and RAM. Leave screens and internal cards to the tech.
41.why: Batteries and RAM are usually reached through an outside cover or latch, so users can replace them. Screens, card readers and Mini-PCIe cards need a technician.

42.tip: Big media sync = fast links: Wi-Fi or a USB cable.
42.why: Syncing apps, movies and music moves lots of data, so it's done over a USB cable or Wi-Fi. Bluetooth and NFC are too slow, and cellular costs data.

43.tip: Inkjet: cheap to buy, wet ink. Laser: dry toner, fused by heat.
43.why: Inkjets cost less to buy at first. Laser printers melt dry toner onto the paper, so pages come out dry, while inkjet ink can still be wet and smear.

44.cue: collate option and prints two copies
44.why: Collating prints each copy as a full set in order, so you get pages 1, 2, 3 and then 1, 2, 3 again. Without collate you'd get 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3.

45.cue: printing takes too long, graphics and photographs
45.tip: Big pictures need memory. More printer RAM = faster big jobs.
45.why: Graphics and photos make large print jobs. More printer RAM lets the printer hold and process the whole page faster instead of waiting on data.

46.cue: Windows print server services to MAC OS
46.tip: Bonjour = Apple's 'hello' service that lets Windows share printers with Macs.
46.why: Bonjour Print Server is Apple software you install on Windows so the Windows PC can share its printers with Mac clients. AirPrint is for Apple devices printing directly.

47.tip: Maintenance kit = parts that wear: fuser and rollers (pickup + transfer).
47.why: Parts that wear out with use, like the fuser assembly and the pickup and transfer rollers, come in the kit. Coronas and paper trays usually aren't included.

48.tip: Damp air = damp paper = paper jams.
48.why: Paper soaks up moisture from humid air, so it sticks together and curls, which causes jams. A test page jamming points to the paper, not the driver or cables.

49.cue: host multiple operating systems on a single CPU
49.tip: Many OSes on one physical server = virtualization.
49.why: Virtualization runs several virtual machines, each with its own OS, on one physical server, so each customer gets a web server without buying separate hardware.

50.tip: VMs don't care what hardware they land on. Restore anywhere.
50.why: A virtual machine runs on a hypervisor, not directly on the hardware, so you can restore it on any server without needing an exact hardware match.

51.tip: Data center = Type 1 (bare metal): ESXi and Hyper-V. Desktop apps like VirtualBox are Type 2.
51.why: VMware ESXi and Hyper-V are Type 1 hypervisors that run directly on server hardware, which suits data centers. Virtual PC, Fusion and VirtualBox run on top of a desktop OS.

52.cue: opens them in different virtual desktops
52.tip: Windows 10 lets you make several desktops (Task View). That's Windows Virtual Desktop.
52.why: Windows 10 lets you create multiple virtual desktops on the same computer and put different apps on each one, then switch between them.

53.tip: PaaS = Platform for building apps. SaaS = use apps. IaaS = rent servers.
53.why: Platform as a Service gives developers the tools and environment to build, test and deliver apps over the web, without managing the servers underneath.

54.tip: SDRAM is synchronized with the clock, so it can pipeline: overlapping work in parallel.
54.why: SDRAM runs in sync with the system clock, which lets it pipeline commands so it handles overlapping instructions at the same time. Two reads and writes per cycle is DDR.

55.tip: After a power outage, check power first: the external RAID box may be off.
55.why: An external RAID controller has its own power. After an outage it may not have come back on, so the server can't see it and reports RAID not found.

56.cue: touch screen that is not working correctly
56.tip: Touch screen slow or odd? Start simple: close apps first, then think hardware.
56.why: With too many apps open, the device runs short of memory and processing power, so taps can lag or register wrong. Closing apps is the first easy fix to try.

57.cue: sharing printers in a corporate environment
57.tip: Shared printer risks: who can print (authentication) and what it remembers (cached files).
57.why: Without user authentication anyone can use or misuse the printer, and cached print files stored on the printer can leak private documents.

58.tip: Assess = look at the impact on the business before the change.
58.why: The assessment step studies how a proposed change will affect business processes, its risks and cost, before anyone approves or carries it out.

59.why: RAID 10 mirrors pairs of drives for safety and then stripes data across the pairs for speed, combining RAID 1 and RAID 0.

60.tip: RAID 1 = one copy, the mirror image.
60.why: RAID 1 writes the same data to two drives, a mirror. If one drive fails, the other still has everything.

61.tip: RAID 5 = stripes + one parity. Needs 3+ drives.
61.why: RAID 5 spreads data across drives with parity info, so the array can rebuild data if any one drive fails.

62.tip: RAID 0 = zero protection, just striping for speed.
62.why: RAID 0 splits data across drives for speed but keeps no copy or parity, so one failed drive loses everything.

63.tip: RAID 6 = RAID 5 with double parity. Survives 2 drive failures.
63.why: RAID 6 stores two sets of parity, so the array keeps working even if two drives fail at the same time.

64.tip: Batteries contain toxic metals: always recycle by local rules.
64.why: Batteries contain toxic metals that can harm people and the environment, so they must be recycled following local regulations, never thrown away or burned.

65.tip: E-waste rule: recycle it, following local regulations.
65.why: Monitors can hold hazardous materials like lead or mercury, so they go to approved e-waste recycling as local rules require.

66.cue: dispose of an old power supply
66.tip: Any computer part? Recycle following local regulations. Never burn or bury.
66.why: Power supplies contain metals and components that shouldn't go in a landfill. Recycling them by local rules keeps hazardous materials out of the environment.

67.tip: Circuit boards are e-waste: recycle them by local rules.
67.why: RAM is a circuit board with metals and chemicals, so it counts as e-waste and should be recycled following local regulations.

68.why: Motherboards contain lead solder and other hazardous materials, so they must go to e-waste recycling according to local regulations.

69.cue: dispose of an old hard drive
69.tip: Hard drive: wipe the data, then recycle by local rules.
69.why: Hard drives are e-waste and should be recycled following local regulations, after you make sure any data on them is securely wiped or destroyed.

70.tip: Random reboots = Power or heat: PSU and CPU.
70.why: A failing power supply can drop power and restart the PC, and an overheating CPU makes the system shut down or reboot to protect itself.

71.why: Unstable power from a bad power supply, or a CPU that overheats, are the classic causes of a computer rebooting on its own.

72.cue: reboots several times before it eventually starts
72.tip: Random reboots? Think PP: Power supply and Processor.
72.why: A failing power supply can drop voltage and cause restarts, and an overheating or faulty CPU can make the PC reset. BIOS, ROM and NICs don't usually cause reboot loops.

73.cue: working on a spreadsheet, the computer reboots
73.tip: Sudden reboot during work = power or heat. Power supply and CPU.
73.why: If the power supply can't deliver steady power, or the CPU overheats, the computer shuts down and restarts on its own to protect itself.

74.why: NetBIOS over TCP/IP uses ports 137 to 139 for names and sessions on older Windows networks. SMB runs on 445 and HTTPS on 443.

75.why: SSH uses port 22 to give a secure, encrypted remote command line. Telnet does the same job on port 23 but without encryption.

76.why: IMAP uses port 143 to let email clients read mail that stays on the server.

77.why: Telnet uses port 23 for remote command line access. It sends everything in plain text, which is why SSH on port 22 replaced it.

78.why: SNMP, Simple Network Management Protocol, uses UDP port 161 so management software can monitor and manage network devices.

79.tip: LDAP = 389: the directory lookup (like Active Directory).
79.why: LDAP uses port 389 to look up users, computers and other objects in a directory service like Active Directory.

80.why: SMTP uses port 25 to send email between mail servers and from clients to servers.

81.tip: SLP = 427: Service Location Protocol finds services like printers.
81.why: SLP, Service Location Protocol, uses port 427 so devices can find services on the local network, like printers, without manual setup.

82.why: DNS uses port 53 to translate names like www.example.com into IP addresses. DHCP uses 67/68 and TFTP uses 69.

83.tip: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and swap ONE run of all-zero groups for ::.
83.why: Remove leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0008 to 8, 0001 to 1) and replace the three 0000 groups with :: to get 2001:db8::a0b0:8:1.

84.tip: Use :: for the LONGEST run of zeros. A single 0000 becomes just 0.
84.why: Drop leading zeros (09ea to 9ea, 0fe0 to fe0, 0290 to 290). The lone 0000 becomes 0, and the two zero groups in a row become ::.

85.tip: Only LEADING zeros go. Trailing zeros (c400) stay.
85.why: Drop leading zeros (0042 to 42, 0010 to 10, 0909 to 909), keep c400 as it is, and replace the three 0000 groups with ::.

86.tip: One zero group can still be written as ::. Leading zeros drop, trailing ones stay.
86.why: Drop leading zeros in each group (0420 to 420, 00c4 to c4, 0025 to 25, 0190 to 190, 0990 to 990) and replace the single 0000 group with ::.

87.tip: Two zero runs? Use :: for the longer one, write the other as 0.
87.why: The two 0000 groups after db8 become ::. The later single 0000 becomes 0. Leading zeros drop (0ab8 to ab8, 0001 to 1), but 1000 keeps its zeros.

88.tip: Three zero groups after fe80 collapse to ::. Then trim leading zeros.
88.why: The three 0000 groups become ::, and leading zeros drop (0220 to 220, 0b3f to b3f, 0029 to 29), giving fe80::220:b3f:f0e0:29.

89.tip: Only one :: is allowed per address. Other zero groups become 0.
89.why: Both 0000 groups are single, so one becomes :: and the other is written 0. Leading zeros drop (00bf to bf, 00e0 to e0) while 9ea0 keeps its trailing zero.

90.cue: contents of RAM have been saved to a temporary file
90.tip: S4 = hibernate: RAM saved to disk, power off.
90.why: In S4, hibernate, the PC copies RAM to a file on the hard drive and powers off. When you turn it on, the saved state is loaded back.

91.tip: S1 = lightest sleep: CPU and RAM still powered.
91.why: S1 is the lightest sleep state: the CPU and RAM keep power and only unused devices turn off, so it wakes very quickly.

92.cue: CPU is off, but the RAM is refreshed
92.tip: S2 = CPU off, RAM still refreshed. One step deeper than S1.
92.why: In S2 the CPU is turned off but the RAM keeps being refreshed so its contents stay. It's deeper than S1 but lighter than S3.

93.tip: S5 = soft off. S0 = on. Count up as it goes deeper.
93.why: S5 is the soft off state: the computer is shut down and nothing is saved, though the power supply still gives a little power for wake-up.

94.tip: S3 = Suspend to RAM (Sleep). S4 = suspend to disk.
94.why: S3, suspend to RAM, turns off the CPU and keeps RAM on slow refresh using little power. It's the normal sleep mode most people use.

95.cue: computer is on and the CPU is running
95.why: S0 is the working state: the computer is fully on and the CPU is running normally.

96.tip: Big photo jobs crawl? Give the printer more RAM.
96.why: High resolution photos create huge print jobs. More RAM in the printer lets it hold and process each page faster. Ribbons are only for impact printers.

97.cue: deep in a mine, paper constantly jams
97.tip: Mine = damp. Damp paper = jams. Move to drier air.
97.why: Mines are very humid, and paper absorbs moisture, then sticks and curls and jams. Moving the printer to a drier place fixes it.

98.tip: Streaks? Shake the toner cartridge to spread the toner out.
98.why: When toner clumps or runs low in parts of the cartridge, the page gets streaks. Gently rocking the cartridge spreads the toner evenly again.

99.cue: not showing up on the list of available printers
99.tip: Can't find the printer? Add it by its IP address.
99.why: If automatic discovery doesn't find a network printer, you can add it manually by typing its IP address so the computer knows where to send jobs.

100.tip: Jobs go out but never print? They're going out the wrong port.
100.why: If the printer driver points to the wrong port, jobs are sent somewhere the printer isn't listening. Changing the port in printer properties fixes it.

101.cue: colors are different from the colors on screens
101.tip: Screen and paper colors don't match? Calibrate.
101.why: Calibration adjusts the printer so its colors line up with what you see on screen, by aligning heads and correcting color output.

102.cue: preventive maintenance, printer no longer available
102.tip: After maintenance, check the basics first: is it plugged in?
102.why: After maintenance the printer may have been left unplugged or turned off. Checking power is the simplest first step before anything else.

103.tip: Faded print = low toner. Replace the cartridge.
103.why: When the toner cartridge runs low, not enough toner reaches the page, so prints look faded. A new cartridge fixes it.

104.tip: Failed to print = the path is broken: loose cable or the share is gone.
104.why: The job can't reach the printer if the cable is loose or disconnected, or if the network printer has stopped being shared. Either one breaks the path to the printer.

105.tip: Garbage characters = bad translation (driver) or bad link (loose cable).
105.why: The driver translates documents into the printer's language. A wrong or old driver, or a loose cable that garbles data, makes strange characters print.

106.tip: Wrong colors? Check the ink: wrong cartridge or dirty print heads.
106.why: Colors come from the ink cartridges and the print heads. A wrong cartridge or clogged, uncalibrated heads mix the colors badly. Cables and ports don't change colors.

107.tip: Faded = not enough toner sticks: low toner or the wrong paper.
107.why: When toner runs low there isn't enough to make dark prints. Paper the printer doesn't support may not hold the toner well, so the print looks pale.

108.tip: Blank panel? Is it on? Is the contrast turned down?
108.why: A blank control panel usually means the printer is off, or the screen's contrast is set so low you can't see anything.

109.tip: Creased paper = paper problem: loose tray guides or paper loaded wrong.
109.why: If the tray guides aren't snug against the paper, or the paper is loaded wrong, it feeds at an angle and gets creased on its way through.

110.tip: Impact printer + faded = ribbon (worn or damaged).
110.why: Impact printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper. When the ribbon is worn out or damaged, there's not enough ink and the characters look faint.

111.tip: Won't feed? Bad paper (wrinkled) or wrong size set.
111.why: Wrinkled paper won't pick up cleanly, and if the printer expects a different paper size than what's loaded, it won't feed from that tray.

112.cue: NVMe drive (C:) and a mechanical hard drive (D:)
112.tip: Missing drive? Look in Disk Management: the OS's view of every disk.
112.why: Disk Management shows every drive Windows can see, even ones without a drive letter or partition, so it tells you if the OS recognizes the disk.

113.cue: save an email attachment, D: drive not an option
113.tip: Quick check: open File Explorer and see if the drive is listed.
113.why: File Explorer lists the drives Windows has mounted. If D: shows there, the OS sees it. Ping, ipconfig and web browsers test networks, not drives.

114.cue: drive, present in the save options yesterday
114.tip: Device Manager = does Windows see the hardware?
114.why: Device Manager lists the hardware Windows detects and shows errors on devices, so you can check if the drive is recognized and its driver works.

115.cue: SSD for the operating system, mechanical hard drive
115.tip: Is the drive there? File Explorer shows it at a glance.
115.why: File Explorer shows all drives Windows has mounted. If the data drive is listed there, the OS recognizes it. Swapping cables is a hardware step, not an OS check.

116.tip: GPS dead? The location service may be turned off.
116.why: GPS depends on the location service. If that service is disabled in settings, GPS won't work even though the hardware is fine.

117.tip: App stuck? Restart the app. Then the device, if needed.
117.why: An app that won't load may be frozen in the background. Closing and restarting it clears its state and usually fixes the problem.

118.tip: Not responding = force close and restart the app.
118.why: When an app hangs, restarting it clears whatever it got stuck on. Screen and GPU problems don't cause a single app to freeze.

119.tip: Can't decrypt = missing the key. Keys live in digital certificates.
119.why: Encrypted email is unlocked with a key from a digital certificate. If that certificate is missing from the device, the email can't be decrypted.

120.tip: Cisco ASA = Adaptive Security Appliance, a stateful firewall box.
120.why: A Cisco ASA is a dedicated firewall that tracks the state of each connection, giving a small company stateful firewall services.

121.tip: Order: Winload finds partition, loads NTOSKRNL and HAL, reads registry and drivers, then the KERNEL takes over.
121.why: After Winload reads the registry and loads device drivers, its job is done, so it hands control to the Windows kernel (NTOSKRNL.EXE).

122.tip: Can't decrypt email? You're missing the right certificate (the key).
122.why: Encrypted email needs the right digital certificate to decrypt it. Installing that certificate lets the laptop open the message.

123.cue: print from laptops and tablets, wireless
123.tip: Printing wirelessly: Wi-Fi (802.11) or Bluetooth. NFC is just a tap, ZigBee is for smart home.
123.why: Laptops and tablets almost all have Wi-Fi (802.11) and Bluetooth, and printers support both for wireless printing. Cellular, ZigBee and NFC aren't used for normal printing.

124.tip: Motherboard must FIT 3 things: the case (size), the power supply (connectors) and the CPU (socket).
124.why: A new board has to fit in the case, get the right connectors from the existing power supply, and have a socket and chipset that work with your CPU. The brand doesn't matter.

125.cue: features of protocols within the TCP/IP stack
125.tip: TCP = Trusty (resends lost data). UDP = Ultra fast, Don't care about Packets lost.
125.why: TCP waits for acknowledgments and resends data that isn't confirmed. UDP skips that checking so it's faster, which suits streaming where a little loss is fine.

126.cue: key on the keyboard is not responding
126.tip: Sticky key = dirt under it. Blow it out with compressed air.
126.why: Dust and crumbs under a key often stop it from working. Compressed air blows the dirt out without taking the keyboard apart.

keys.k: does not print a test page

127.tip: Driver = translator. Bad translator prints gibberish or nothing at all.
127.why: The driver turns your document into commands the printer understands. With the wrong driver the printer gets garbled commands, so it prints strange characters or fails the test page.

128.cue: change the wireless router IP address
128.tip: Default settings are public knowledge. Change the default IP so attackers can't guess it.
128.why: Every router of a model ships with the same default IP address, which anyone can look up. Changing it makes it harder for someone to find and log in to the router.

129.tip: Airplane mode turns off radios. Check it first when GPS is dead.
129.why: Airplane mode can switch off wireless radios, including location services. Make sure it is off so GPS can work.

130.cue: laptop and GPS is not functioning
130.tip: GPS broken? First check that the location service is turned ON.
130.why: GPS depends on the location service being enabled. If the service is off or not running, apps can't get a location, so you check its status first.

131.cue: limit the amount of data that the CPU can receive
131.tip: Cache = the CPU's own pocket. A small pocket holds less data at once.
131.why: Cache is very fast memory right on the CPU. Its size limits how much data the CPU can keep close at hand and work on at one time.

132.cue: optical drive greatest amount of storage
132.tip: BD-RE = Blu-ray Rewritable: biggest discs, and it can read and write CDs and DVDs too.
132.why: Blu-ray discs hold the most data, and a BD-RE drive can rewrite them. It also reads and writes older CDs and DVDs. BD-ROM can only read.

133.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 10)
133.tip: Welcome screen = finish line. Nothing comes after it in the boot process.
133.why: Showing the Welcome (logon) screen is the last step of booting. Windows is fully loaded and just waits for you to sign in.

134.tip: sfc = System File Checker: scans and fixes protected system files.
134.why: System File Checker scans the protected Windows system files and replaces damaged or wrong versions with correct copies.

135.tip: DISM = Deployment Image Servicing and Management: it fixes images.
135.why: DISM services Windows images, including the recovery image, so it can repair and prepare the image Windows runs from.

136.tip: tasklist = list tasks (processes). taskkill = end them.
136.why: tasklist shows the processes running on a local or remote computer, with their process IDs.

137.tip: taskkill kills tasks by PID or name.
137.why: taskkill stops one or more running processes, chosen by process ID or by image (program) name.

138.tip: msconfig = Microsoft config: choose what runs at startup.
138.why: msconfig, System Configuration, lets you choose startup options and which programs and services load when Windows starts.

139.tip: dir = directory listing: shows the files here.
139.why: dir lists the files and folders in the current directory.

140.why: gpupdate forces the PC to pull and apply the latest Group Policy settings instead of waiting for the next refresh.

141.tip: gpresult = group policy results: see what really applied.
141.why: gpresult shows which Group Policy settings are applied to the user and computer, so you can check settings you suspect are wrong.

keys.k: change from the current working folder

142.why: cd moves you from the current folder to another folder in the command prompt.

143.tip: NORTHbridge = the fast stuff up top: RAM and video. SOUTHbridge = slow stuff: drives, sound, I/O ports.
143.why: The Northbridge handles the high speed links between the CPU, RAM and the video card. Slower devices like hard drives, sound and I/O ports go through the Southbridge.

144.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 8)
144.tip: Welcome screen = finish line, in every Windows version.
144.why: When WINLOGON.EXE shows the Welcome screen, Windows has finished loading. Booting is complete and the PC waits for a user to log in.

145.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 7)
145.tip: Welcome screen = the last stop. The card reader detail is just noise.
145.why: Displaying the Welcome screen is the final boot step. Extra hardware like a media card reader doesn't change the boot order.

146.cue: restore point, reverse the software installation
146.tip: Restore point -> System Restore. It rolls back the system, not your files.
146.why: System Restore returns Windows settings, programs and drivers to an earlier restore point, but leaves your personal files alone. That undoes the failed install.

147.tip: Before upgrading ask 2 things: Will my APPS run? Will my HARDWARE meet the minimum?
147.why: Old PCs may not have enough RAM or a fast enough CPU for Windows 10, and old or custom programs may not run on it. Both must be checked before upgrading.

148.cue: wireless router settings should be disabled
148.tip: Turn OFF the 3 'easy' features: UPnP, WPS and SSID broadcast. Easy for you is easy for hackers.
148.why: UPnP lets devices open ports without asking, WPS PINs can be cracked, and broadcasting the SSID advertises your network. MAC filtering and parental controls add security.

149.tip: DNS spoofing = the phone book lies: strange DNS server, and the right name takes you to the wrong site.
149.why: DNS turns names into IP addresses. If an attacker fakes DNS, nslookup shows a DNS server you don't recognize and typing cisco.com sends you to a different site.

150.tip: Mantrap = two doors, one person at a time. No tailgaters.
150.why: A mantrap is a small room with two doors where only one opens at a time, so a second person can't follow someone in.

151.tip: Cloud = rent, don't buy. Less gear and training to pay for, no upgrade or license bills.
151.why: With IaaS and ITaaS the provider owns the equipment and handles upgrades and licenses. You spend less on local hardware, training and software costs.

152.tip: Stop cell data: flip Airplane mode, or switch off Mobile data in Settings.
152.why: Airplane mode turns off all radios, including cellular. The mobile data switch in Settings turns off just cellular data. A hotspot or VPN still uses data.

153.cue: bootable USB hard drive, loads Windows
153.tip: Want to boot from it? Put it FIRST in the boot order. USB hard disk, not USB key.
153.why: The BIOS tries devices in boot order and uses the first one that can boot. Moving the USB Hard Disk option to the top makes it boot Linux whenever the drive is plugged in.

154.tip: Beep codes are a hardware Morse code from POST. Each count points to a different part.
154.why: During POST the BIOS beeps in patterns to report hardware problems it finds, like bad RAM or video. The codes differ between BIOS makers, so you look them up.

155.cue: Microsoft 365, virtual servers leased from a local data center
155.tip: Leased servers in a local data center used only by the college = private cloud.
155.why: The college's own servers, storage and directory run on virtual servers leased just for it, with access control managed locally. Resources used by one organization form a private cloud.

156.cue: displays the Windows installation program screen again
156.tip: Start simple: is the install disc still in the drive?
156.why: If the install disc is still in the drive and boots first, the PC loads the setup program again. Checking the most obvious, easy cause first is good troubleshooting.

157.cue: connect from smart phones, tablets, and laptops
157.tip: Phones and tablets have no Ethernet port. Wireless needs an Access Point.
157.why: An access point lets wireless devices join the wired company network. Phones and tablets connect only by Wi-Fi, so a switch or hub wouldn't help them.

158.tip: Active = it moves (fans use power). Passive = just sits there (heat sink, thermal paste).
158.why: Active cooling uses powered parts, like fans, to move heat away. A heat sink and thermal paste are passive because they cool without using power.

159.tip: Too little RAM = Windows borrows the slow hard drive (paging). Slow drive, slow PC.
159.why: When RAM is full, Windows moves data to a page file on the hard drive. The drive is much slower than RAM, so swapping often makes the computer slow.

160.tip: Shared printers don't appear by magic: each user uses Add a printer and picks it.
160.why: Other users must connect to the shared printer. Using Add a printer and choosing the shared HP printer installs it and its driver from the host PC automatically.

161.cue: separate power connection to directly power the CPU
161.tip: ATX12V = ATX plus an extra 12V plug just for the CPU.
161.why: ATX12V is the most common power supply type. It adds a separate 12 volt connector on the motherboard that feeds the CPU directly. EPS12V is mainly for servers.

162.cue: dialog box pops up requesting a file name
162.tip: Asked for a file name when printing? You're 'printing' to a file, a virtual printer like Print to PDF.
162.why: A virtual printer, such as Microsoft Print to PDF, saves the print job as a file instead of sending it to paper. It's set as default, so nothing reaches the HP printer.

163.cue: single CPU to perform as though two CPUs
163.tip: Hyper-Threading = one core, two threads. It looks like two CPUs.
163.why: Intel's Hyper-Threading lets one core run two streams of instructions at once, so Windows sees two logical CPUs. HyperTransport is an AMD bus, not this.

164.cue: multiple tenants to share the same storage
164.tip: Pool = shared. Many customers swim in the same pool of resources.
164.why: Resource pooling means the provider puts its storage, processing and bandwidth into one pool and shares it among many customers (tenants) as they need it.

165.cue: external ports to connect an external storage
165.tip: The 'e' in eSATA means external. Plain SATA is internal. DVI and HDMI are for video.
165.why: Thunderbolt, USB and eSATA are external ports that carry data to storage drives. SATA is an internal port, and DVI and HDMI only carry video and audio.

166.tip: Power hungry or internal: graphics card, SATA drive, fans. USB stuff gets power from the port.
166.why: Big graphics cards, internal SATA drives and fans need their own power cables. USB flash drives, keyboards and wireless adapters get power through their port or slot.

167.cue: thin clients be a good choice
167.tip: Thin client = thin on its own power, so it needs a FAT network and strong servers.
167.why: Thin clients do little work themselves and rely on servers over the network. They fit low power devices and places with fast LANs and powerful servers, not slow rural links.

168.tip: Type 1 runs on bare metal servers: vSphere, Oracle VM Server. Type 2 runs on a desktop OS: VirtualBox, Workstation.
168.why: The exhibit shows a hypervisor running directly on the hardware (Type 1). VMware vSphere and Oracle VM Server are Type 1. VirtualBox, Virtual PC and Workstation run on top of an OS.

169.cue: can print to the local network printer, but cannot access the cloud
169.tip: Local works, internet fails? Check the gateway. Here it's 192.168.100.1, outside the 192.168.0.x network.
169.why: The PC has 192.168.0.20 /24 but its default gateway is 192.168.100.1, which isn't on its network. Local printing works, but traffic to the internet can't leave. DHCP handed out that gateway.

170.cue: smartwatch shows that it is in discoverable mode
170.tip: Smartwatch pairs over Bluetooth. Watch discoverable but no link? The phone's Bluetooth is off.
170.why: Smartwatches pair with phones over Bluetooth. The watch is ready to be found, so if the phone's Bluetooth is turned off the app can't see or connect to it.

171.cue: DDR SDRAM fastest clock rate, least power
171.tip: Higher DDR number = faster and lower voltage. DDR4 beats DDR3 and DDR2. GDDR5 is for video cards.
171.why: Each new DDR generation runs faster and uses less voltage. DDR4 is the newest here, so it's fastest and most efficient. GDDR5 is graphics memory, not system RAM.

172.tip: The picture is a UEFI/BIOS setup screen. There you set BIOS passwords, not Wi-Fi or screen settings.
172.why: The exhibit shows the UEFI BIOS setup utility. In its security section you can set passwords that control who can enter the BIOS. Screen and Wi-Fi settings are in Windows.

173.cue: short or a termination error in the wiring
173.tip: Cable problem? Cable tester. Shorts, opens, bad wiring: it checks every wire.
173.why: A cable tester checks each wire in a network cable for shorts, breaks and wrong pin order. A tone generator just finds which cable is which.

174.why: Port 110 is the well known port for POP3, the protocol a client uses to download email from a mail server.

175.tip: taskKILL kills tasks. tasklist only lists them.
175.why: taskkill stops running processes, using either their process ID (PID) or their program name. tasklist is the command that just shows what is running.

176.cue: partition scheme that supports storing a backup
176.tip: GPT keeps a Guaranteed Partition Table backup. MBR has only one copy.
176.why: GPT stores a main partition table at the start of the disk and a backup copy at the end. If one gets damaged, the other can be used to recover.

177.cue: MBR be partitioned to support additional logical drives
177.tip: MBR has 4 slots. Turn one into an EXTENDED partition, a box that holds logical drives.
177.why: MBR allows only four primary partitions. Making one of them an extended partition lets you create many logical drives inside it.

178.cue: simple text file, created in Notepad
178.tip: Windows built-ins: PowerShell (.ps1) and batch files (.bat). Bash and C++ are not built in.
178.why: Windows has two built-in script runners: PowerShell and the command line batch interpreter. Both can run commands saved in a plain text file.

179.cue: variables contained in the sample.sh script
179.tip: 'read uname' = the script asks you, so it's input. $HOSTNAME and $HOME come from the system.
179.why: The script uses 'read uname' to store what you type, so $uname is an input variable made in the script. $HOSTNAME isn't set in the script, Linux sets it as an environment variable.

180.cue: lawyer need to use the tracert command
180.tip: tracert = trace the route, hop by hop.
180.why: tracert lists each router on the path to the destination. ping only tests reachability, and netstat lists connections.

181.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, cellular SIM)
181.tip: Kernel takes over -> NTOSKRNL starts WINLOGON -> Welcome screen. K then L: Kernel, then Login.
181.why: Once the kernel (NTOSKRNL.EXE) is in control, it starts WINLOGON.EXE, which then shows the Welcome screen so you can sign in.

182.cue: secure method of erasing the data
182.tip: Flash memory isn't magnetic, so degaussing does nothing. Use secure erase software.
182.why: Secure erase tools overwrite every memory cell so data can't be recovered. A quick format only removes the file list, and magnets don't affect flash drives.

183.cue: contents of the ite_user home directory

keys.k: two data files and three directories

183.tip: In ls -l, a leading '-' is a file and 'd' is a directory. Count: 2 dashes, 3 d's.
183.why: The listing shows January and February starting with '-' (files) and Newfiles, Test1 and Test2 starting with 'd' (directories). The files have sizes, so they do hold data.

184.tip: Live Tiles are alive: they show messages, news and photos.
184.why: This is a Windows phone Start screen with Live Tiles. Each tile can show live content like messages, news and photos. Unpinning a tile does not uninstall the app.

185.tip: PHI leaves the clinic = breach. Screenshots of records or copies of patient data sent away both count.
185.why: Protected health information can't be shared or copied outside the clinic without permission. Screenshots of real records and backups moved to an IT office both expose patient data.

186.tip: del = DELete files. rd removes directories, move relocates files.
186.why: The del command deletes one or more files in a Windows directory. Removing an empty directory is rd, and relocating a file is move.

187.tip: Frozen app? Do what you'd do with any frozen device: reset it.
187.why: A reset (restart) clears memory and stops stuck processes, so an app that isn't responding usually works again. Turning off Bluetooth or Wi-Fi won't fix a hung app.

188.cue: recover an older version of a document
188.tip: File History = history of your FILES. System Restore = system settings, not documents.
188.why: File History saves copies of your files over time, so you can open an earlier version from the same day. System Restore doesn't touch personal files.

189.cue: change the file system to NTFS without losing the data
189.tip: convert X: /fs:ntfs turns FAT32 into NTFS and keeps your files.
189.why: The convert command changes a FAT32 drive to NTFS in place, keeping the files on it. Reformatting or making a new partition would erase the data.

190.cue: local backup of iPhone data on a Windows laptop
190.tip: iPhone + Windows = iTunes. Finder and Time Machine are Mac tools.
190.why: On a Windows PC, Apple's iTunes is used to back up and sync an iPhone. Finder and Time Machine only exist on Macs, and Google sync is for Android.

191.tip: Storage Spaces = pool your drives into one big space, like software RAID.
191.why: Storage Spaces lets you group several drives into a storage pool and set them up as arrays that can protect data, similar to RAID, all from inside Windows.

192.cue: not restored when using Windows Restore
192.tip: Restore fixes the SYSTEM, never your stuff. Your documents stay as they are.
192.why: A restore point covers system files, drivers, the registry and program settings. Personal data files are left alone, so they aren't rolled back or lost.

193.tip: Boot order starts: POST, then BIOS reads CMOS settings, then it finds a boot drive.
193.why: After the power-on self-test checks hardware, the BIOS reads its saved settings from CMOS memory, such as the boot order, before it looks for a drive to boot from.

194.tip: More cores = more work at once. Great for games and video editing.
194.why: A multicore CPU runs several tasks in parallel, so it finishes work faster than a single core. Heavy apps like games and video editors take advantage of that.

195.tip: MAC = burned into the NIC, never changes. To reach the internet you need a public IP.
195.why: A MAC address is built into the network card, so it stays the same on every network. Internet routers only forward public addresses, so a public IPv4 or IPv6 address is required.

196.cue: laptop screen flickers and appears dull
196.tip: External monitor fine, laptop screen dim? The light is the problem: backlight or inverter.
196.why: The external monitor looks normal, so the GPU works. A dim, flickering laptop screen points to its lighting: the backlight or the inverter that powers it.

197.tip: New power supply: does it FIT (size) and is it STRONG enough (wattage)?
197.why: The replacement has to fit in the case and give enough watts to run every part in the computer. UPS and eSATA support aren't power supply features.

198.tip: Unbuffered = no middleman. Data goes straight to the CPU, so it's faster. Buffered is for big servers.
198.why: Buffered RAM has an extra chip between the memory and the controller, which adds a small delay. Unbuffered RAM is read directly, so it's faster for home and gaming PCs.

199.cue: UTM appliance, such as a Cisco ASA 5506-X
199.tip: UTM = Unified Threat Management: security tools in one box, like firewall plus IPS/IDS.
199.why: A UTM appliance combines several security devices, including a stateful firewall and an intrusion prevention or detection system. It isn't a modem, storage drive or big switch.

200.cue: replaces the memory, does not resolve the performance
200.tip: Fix didn't work? Write it down and put the original part back before trying the next idea.
200.why: Since the new memory didn't help, you put the original memory back so you don't add new variables, and you document that this attempt failed before testing the next cause.

201.cue: VirtualBox to run automatically when Windows 10 starts
201.tip: Want it to start with Windows? Drop its shortcut in the Startup folder.
201.why: Windows runs every shortcut in the Startup folder when you sign in. Task Manager's Startup tab can only enable or disable programs already listed, not add new ones.

202.cue: web-based application was no longer functioning
202.tip: Before you leave: VERIFY that everything works, not just the thing you fixed.
202.why: After a fix you must test the whole system. The new antivirus likely broke the web app, and checking full system functionality would have caught it before leaving.

203.tip: Hotend: heat depends on the filament, and nozzles wear out like ink.
203.why: Each filament type melts at its own temperature, so the nozzle heats to match. Nozzles wear and clog over time, so they're consumables you replace in normal maintenance.

204.cue: What can be determined from the output
204.tip: January is -rw-rw-r--: r for owner, r for group, r for others. Everyone can read.
204.why: The permissions for January are rw- for owner, rw- for group and r-- for others. Each group has an r, so all three can read the file. There are 2 files and 3 directories.

205.cue: very fast boot and high capacity storage
205.tip: SSHD = SSD + HDD in one drive: SSD speed for booting, HDD space for storage.
205.why: A solid state hybrid drive has a small flash section for fast access, like booting, and a large spinning disk for lots of storage. It mixes both benefits.

206.cue: require the width of two slots
206.tip: Big fans and heat sinks = graphics card. That's why it takes two slots.
206.why: Powerful graphics cards make a lot of heat, so they carry large heat sinks and fans. That cooling makes them two slots wide even though they plug into one PCIe x16 slot.

207.tip: Discoverable = saying 'Hi, I'm Speaker X, and here's what I can do.'
207.why: In discoverable mode a Bluetooth device broadcasts its name and what it supports, so the laptop can list it and start pairing. A PIN may come later, not in the broadcast.

208.cue: BIOS locates and reads the configuration settings

keys.k: first drive that contains a valid boot sector

208.tip: POST, read CMOS, then boot from the FIRST drive with a valid boot sector.
208.why: Once the BIOS has read its CMOS settings, it follows the boot order and starts from the first drive that has a valid boot sector.

209.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, SIM slot)
209.tip: Kernel in charge -> it starts WINLOGON. Kernel, then Login.
209.why: After the Windows kernel takes control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE, the program that handles the logon and shows the Welcome screen.

210.tip: bootrec = BOOT RECovery. It fixes the MBR and boot records.
210.why: bootrec is a recovery tool that repairs boot problems, such as a damaged master boot record (bootrec /fixmbr). diskpart manages drives and format prepares them.

211.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, 4 GB RAM)
211.tip: Kernel takes over -> starts WINLOGON -> Welcome screen. The 4 GB RAM detail doesn't matter.
211.why: Right after the kernel takes control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE. The Welcome screen comes one step later, after WINLOGON runs.

212.tip: gpRESULT shows the RESULT of group policy. gpUPDATE refreshes it.
212.why: gpresult displays which group policy settings are applied to the user and computer, so you can check settings you think are wrong. gpupdate applies new policies.

213.cue: WinLoad loads two files: NTOSKRNL.EXE and HAL.DLL
213.tip: Winload order: find partition, load kernel and HAL, read REGISTRY and drivers, hand to kernel.
213.why: After loading NTOSKRNL.EXE and HAL.DLL, Winload reads the registry, picks a hardware profile and loads the drivers. Only then does the kernel take over.

214.cue: control of the boot process is given to Windows Boot Manager
214.tip: Boot Manager (BOOTMGR) points the way, then Winload follows that path to the boot partition.
214.why: Once Windows Boot Manager is running, Winload uses the path that BOOTMGR gives it to find the Windows boot partition, and then it loads the kernel files.

215.tip: App won't load? Restart the device first. Display settings don't stop apps.
215.why: A reset restarts the device, clears memory and ends stuck processes. That often lets an app load again. Display or refresh settings don't affect whether apps load.

216.cue: file system that supports a partition size up to 2 TB
216.tip: FAT32 is the only FILE SYSTEM in the list. Formatting, dynamic and basic disk are not file systems.
216.why: FAT32 is a file system, and the course says its partitions can be up to 2 TB. Formatting is a process, and basic and dynamic disks are disk types, not file systems.

217.cue: Why would a technician need to use the copy command
217.tip: copy = make a duplicate in a new place. move = relocate it.
217.why: The copy command copies files from one location to another, leaving the originals in place. Moving or relocating files is done with move.

218.tip: Moving house: Easy Transfer for one PC, USMT for many. Upgrade Advisor only checks if a PC can upgrade.
218.why: Windows Easy Transfer and the User State Migration Tool (USMT) both copy user files and settings from an old PC to a new one. USMT is the scriptable tool for many PCs.

219.tip: Extend and span? Think dynamic disk: it grows.
219.why: In this course, a disk is converted to dynamic so a volume can grow into free space and be used flexibly. There is no FAT64 file system, so that choice is out.

220.cue: full format more beneficial than a quick format

keys.k: analyzing the disk drive for errors

220.tip: Full format = full checkup: it deletes AND scans for bad sectors. Quick format just deletes.
220.why: A full format removes the files and also scans the whole disk for bad sectors. A quick format only clears the file table, so it skips the error check.

221.tip: Different vendors, different drivers: each PC needs its OWN recovery disc.
221.why: Recovery discs from each vendor hold the drivers and settings for that exact model. Since the PCs come from different vendors and run 32-bit or 64-bit Windows, one disc can't fit them all.

222.cue: remote network installation, unable to communicate
222.tip: PXE = Pre-boot eXecution Environment: the NIC talks to the network before any OS is loaded.
222.why: A network install starts before any OS is on the disk, so the network card itself must boot from the network. That needs a PXE-enabled NIC to reach the deployment server.

223.cue: install Windows on a GPT disk
223.tip: GPT goes with UEFI. MBR goes with old BIOS.
223.why: To boot Windows from a GPT disk, the computer must use UEFI firmware. The 2 TB and 4 primary partition limits are MBR rules, not GPT ones.

224.tip: SIM = System Image Manager: it builds the answer file for unattended installs.
224.why: Windows System Image Manager (SIM) creates the answer file that tells an unattended install which settings, apps and drivers to use.

225.tip: 32 to 64 bit? No upgrade path. Always a clean install.
225.why: You can't upgrade a 32-bit Windows to a 64-bit Windows in place. You have to do a clean install of the 64-bit version, then reinstall apps.

226.tip: Stop the loop, then fix the disk: disable auto restart, then chkdsk /F /R.
226.why: Disabling automatic restart lets you read the error instead of rebooting again. Running chkdsk /F /R fixes file system errors and bad sectors that can stop Windows from loading.

keys.k: SID of the original PC is not cleared

227.tip: Clone without Sysprep = twin SIDs. Same SID on the network causes trouble.
227.why: Each Windows PC needs a unique security identifier (SID). If the image is not generalized with Sysprep first, every clone has the same SID, which causes network problems.

228.cue: files cannot be synced while traveling
228.tip: No company network? Use the cloud: OneDrive bridges the server and the traveler.
228.why: The user can reach the internet but not the company server. Syncing through OneDrive, a cloud service, lets files sync anywhere there is internet.

229.tip: New disk steps: Initialize, then partition, then format.
229.why: A brand new disk has no signature Windows can read. You must initialize it in Disk Management before you can create partitions on it.

230.tip: PRINT$ is a hidden ($) share that holds Printer drivers.
230.why: PRINT$ is a hidden administrative share that stores printer drivers, so clients can download the right driver when they connect to a shared printer.

231.tip: Fix the MBR: bootrec /fixmbr says it right in the name.
231.why: bootrec /fixmbr writes a new master boot record to the disk. sfc fixes system files and chkdsk fixes the file system, not the MBR.

232.tip: Right after POST, the PC reads the MBR/GPT. Fails there = Invalid Boot Disk.
232.why: Right after POST, the computer looks for the MBR or GPT to find the OS. If that is corrupted, it can't find a bootable disk. Drivers and services load much later.

233.why: Virtual Network Computing listens on TCP port 5900. 3389 is Windows Remote Desktop, a different screen sharing protocol.

234.tip: Mac = Screen Sharing. Windows = Remote Desktop and Remote Assistance.
234.why: Screen Sharing is the built-in macOS feature that lets a remote user see and control the Mac. Remote Desktop and Remote Assistance are Windows tools.

235.tip: Operations and planning = what we own and plan to buy: inventory.
235.why: Operations and planning documents track day-to-day resources, such as inventory of hardware and software. Disaster recovery and diagrams belong to other categories.

236.tip: Found illegal content? Call and Write: contact a first responder, document everything. Don't touch or confront.
236.why: You must not destroy evidence or confront anyone. Contact a first responder and write down as much as you can, so the evidence and the chain of custody stay intact.

237.tip: Level one asks Who, What, What changed. Technical outputs come later.
237.why: A level one tech records who the customer is, what the problem is and what changed recently. Diagnostic output and CMOS settings are gathered by higher-level techs.

238.tip: Be polite: let them finish, and ask before you put them on hold.
238.why: Good customer service means listening without interrupting and asking permission before a hold. Interrupting or passing angry callers away right away hurts trust.

239.tip: Angry caller: Listen, then Lead back to the problem.
239.why: Let the angry customer vent without interruption, then steer the talk back to fixing the problem. Matching their anger or transferring at once makes it worse.

240.tip: Escalate when it's too long or too hard for level one.
240.why: Level one handles quick, common fixes. Problems that will take a long time or go beyond level one knowledge are passed to level two techs.

241.tip: Before you market: check policy, ask permission.
241.why: Sending unsolicited emails breaks policy and annoys customers. The tech should have checked the company rules and asked the customer if they wanted that information.

242.tip: RDP: 3389 and encrypted. Port 22 is SSH.
242.why: RDP uses TCP port 3389 and encrypts the session. Port 22 belongs to SSH, and RDP clients exist for Mac, Linux and mobile too.

243.cue: collecting and analyzing data, illegal activity
243.tip: Forensics = CSI for computers: collect and analyze evidence.
243.why: Computer forensics is the collection and analysis of data from systems and storage for a legal investigation. Cyber law is the set of laws, not the investigation.

244.tip: Volatile = vanishes when power goes. RAM is volatile, disks are not.
244.why: Volatile data lives in RAM and CPU caches and is lost when power is removed. Data on magnetic or external drives stays after power off.

245.cue: file shown in the exhibit must be sent
245.tip: Share the file, hide the secrets: omit passwords, send them separately.
245.why: The file contains passwords. You can still share it, but replace the passwords first and give them only through a secure channel if needed.

246.cue: essential for a level one technician
246.tip: Level one skill: Summarize. Turn a long story into a short work order.
246.why: Level one techs must turn the customer's description into a short, clear summary in the work order, so the next tech understands it fast.

247.cue: control illegal use of software and content
247.tip: DRM = Digital Rights Management: locks content against piracy.
247.why: Digital rights management uses technology to stop illegal copying and use of software and media. An EULA is just the license agreement text.

248.tip: SLA = Service Level Agreement: the contract sets the support level.
248.why: A service level agreement is a contract that states how much and what kind of support a customer gets, so it decides the level of help.

249.tip: Possible crime scene? Don't touch. Get the evidence expert.
249.why: This may be a crime scene. Touching the drives or cables could destroy evidence, so find someone trained to collect evidence and keep the chain of custody.

250.cue: scripting language and a compiled language
250.tip: Script = read line by line. Compiled = translated first into an executable.
250.why: Scripts are run by an interpreter one line at a time. Compiled languages must first be turned into executable machine code by a compiler.

251.tip: Multifactor = different kinds: something you know + something you are.
251.why: Multifactor uses two or more different factor types. A password is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are.

252.tip: Renamed system files = virus sign. Scan it, or restore it.
252.why: Renamed system files are a sign of malware. Remove it with antivirus software, or restore the system from a clean backup.

253.tip: Test a theory by changing one thing: new user, no network.
253.why: Logging in as another user tests if the problem is tied to one profile. Unplugging the network tests if an outside attack is involved. The other choices just gather information.

254.tip: BitLocker needs TPM + Two volumes: T and T.
254.why: BitLocker needs at least two volumes (one unencrypted to boot from) and normally a TPM chip to store the keys. EFS is a different, file-level encryption.

255.tip: Asymmetric = two different keys (public and private). Symmetric = same key.
255.why: Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: one key encrypts and the other decrypts. Using identical keys on both ends is symmetric encryption.

256.tip: In this exam: email-spread keystroke recorder = virus.
256.why: A virus can spread as an email attachment and carry a payload, such as a keylogger, that records what you type to steal passwords and data.

257.tip: Stubborn malware? Boot Safe Mode: it loads only the basics, so malware can't hide.
257.why: Safe Mode starts Windows with minimal drivers and programs, so most malware does not run. Then a system restore or scan can remove it.

258.cue: buying supplies for the personal crafting business
258.tip: Personal business on company resources? Check the AUP: Acceptable Use Policy.
258.why: The acceptable use policy says how employees may use company equipment and time. Running a personal business on them breaks that policy.

259.cue: password rules, not part of a domain
259.tip: No domain = local. Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) sets password and lockout rules.
259.why: On a standalone PC with no domain, the Local Security Policy tool sets password length, complexity and account lockout rules.

260.cue: password as soon as it powers on
260.tip: Password before the OS boots = BIOS password.
260.why: The BIOS runs before the operating system, so a password asked for at power on comes from the BIOS or UEFI settings, not the Windows login.

261.cue: increasing the size of the swap
261.tip: Swap is fake RAM on the slow disk. More RAM beats more swap.
261.why: Swap stores inactive RAM content on the hard disk, which is much slower than real RAM. A bigger swap helps a little, but adding RAM is the real fix.

262.tip: GPS knows WHERE: navigate, find nearby places, track the device.
262.why: GPS gives your location, so it powers maps and directions, location-based search results and finding a lost device. Remote wipe and phone lookup don't need GPS.

263.tip: Linux permissions: UGO = User (owner), Group, Others (all users).
263.why: Linux sets read, write and execute permissions for three sets: the owner, the group and all other users.

264.cue: widget is touched an app is launched
264.tip: Widgets are windows into apps. Tap the widget, open the app. Normal.
264.why: A widget is a small view of an app on the home screen. Tapping it opening the full app is expected, not a virus.

265.tip: Sandbox = a play box: the app can't get out to harm the rest.
265.why: A sandbox isolates each app from the OS and other apps, so a malicious app can't reach and infect the rest of the device.

266.tip: Mac backups go back in time: Time Machine.
266.why: Time Machine is the backup tool built into macOS. Deja Dup is a Linux tool, and Disk Utility manages disks rather than backups.

267.tip: Kernel panic = the core crashed. Corrupted drivers crash the core.
267.why: Drivers run inside the kernel, so a corrupted driver can crash it and cause a kernel panic. A missing GRUB would stop boot before the kernel loads.

268.tip: Slow phone? Look for a hungry app running in the background.
268.why: A power-hungry app in the background uses CPU and memory, which slows everything else. Close it to speed the device up.

269.cue: boot an operating system by default
269.tip: Active partition = the one the computer actively boots from.
269.why: The active partition is the one marked to hold the boot files, so the computer boots the OS from it by default.

270.tip: NTFS is huge: 16 exabytes. FAT32 tops out at 2 TB.
270.why: NTFS supports partitions up to 16 exabytes and adds security features like permissions. FAT32 is limited to 2 TB partitions.

271.cue: USB flash drives, files larger than 4 GB
271.tip: exFAT = extended FAT for flash: big files, no 4 GB limit.
271.why: exFAT is made for flash drives and removes the 4 GB file size limit of FAT32, while still working on Windows and Mac.

272.tip: Extended partition is a container: it holds up to 23 logical drives.
272.why: On an MBR disk, one extended partition can be split into as many as 23 logical drives, getting around the 4 primary partition limit.

273.cue: file system for optical disk media
273.tip: CDFS = CD File System, for optical discs.
273.why: CDFS, the Compact Disc File System, is built for optical media like CDs and DVDs.

274.cue: only exist on a hard disk that has an MBR
274.tip: Logical drives live inside an extended partition, an MBR-only idea.
274.why: Logical drives are sections inside an extended partition, and extended partitions only exist on MBR disks. GPT disks don't need them.

275.tip: Basic disk can grow only next door: contiguous space. Dynamic can span.
275.why: A basic disk can extend a partition only into free space right next to it on the same disk. Spanning across disks needs a dynamic disk.

276.tip: Partition = a part of the drive. Like rooms in a house.
276.why: A partition is a section of a hard drive that is set aside and treated as its own area. Formatting then puts a file system on it.

277.cue: 512 bytes long and that contains the boot loader
277.tip: MBR = Master Boot Record: the first 512 bytes, holds the boot loader.
277.why: The master boot record is the first 512 byte sector of the disk. It holds the boot loader and the partition table.

278.cue: volume that can span across more than one disk
278.tip: Dynamic = flexible: volumes can span many disks.
278.why: Dynamic disks support volumes that span, stripe or mirror across more than one physical disk. Basic disks can't do that.

279.cue: NTOSKRNL.EXE starts the login file called WINLOGON.EXE
279.tip: Last two steps: NTOSKRNL starts WINLOGON, then WINLOGON shows Welcome.
279.why: Once the kernel starts WINLOGON.EXE, its job is to show the Welcome or login screen. That is the final step of the boot.

280.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen
280.tip: Welcome screen = the finish line. Nothing comes after.
280.why: Showing the Welcome screen is the last step of the Windows boot process, so there are no more steps.

281.cue: currently working on the following step: POST
281.tip: Boot order start: POST, then CMOS settings, then boot sector.
281.why: After POST checks the hardware, the BIOS reads its configuration settings from CMOS memory, such as the boot order.

282.cue: BIOS locates and reads the configuration settings

keys.k: first drive that contains a valid boot sector

282.tip: CMOS tells the boot order. Then BIOS boots the first drive with a valid boot sector.
282.why: The CMOS settings include the boot order. The BIOS then uses it to boot from the first drive that has a valid boot sector.

283.cue: control of the boot process is given to Windows Boot Manager
283.tip: BOOTMGR points the way: Winload follows its path to the boot partition.
283.why: Windows Boot Manager holds the path to the Windows install. Winload uses that path to find the boot partition before loading the kernel.

284.cue: Winload uses the path specified in BOOTMGR
284.tip: Found the partition? Load the core: NTOSKRNL (kernel) and HAL (hardware layer).
284.why: After finding the boot partition, Winload loads the two core files of Windows: NTOSKRNL.EXE, the kernel, and HAL.DLL, the hardware abstraction layer.

285.tip: Drivers loaded? Winload hands off: the kernel takes over.
285.why: Once Winload has read the registry and loaded the drivers, its work is done and the Windows kernel takes control of the boot.

286.cue: The Windows kernel takes over the boot process

keys.k: starts the login file called WINLOGON.EXE

286.tip: Kernel in charge, then it starts WINLOGON, then Welcome.
286.why: Once the kernel takes over, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE, the program that handles logging in.

287.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen
287.tip: Welcome screen = done. The boot ends there.
287.why: The Welcome screen shown by WINLOGON.EXE is the final step of the boot process, so nothing else follows.

288.cue: The Windows kernel takes over the boot process

keys.k: starts the login file called WINLOGON.EXE

288.tip: Kernel, then WINLOGON, then Welcome screen.
288.why: After the kernel takes control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE, which will then show the Welcome screen.

289.tip: Handshake attack = SYN flood: tons of SYNs, never finishing the handshake.
289.why: A SYN flood sends many SYN requests and never completes the TCP handshake, so the server fills up with half-open connections.

290.tip: Rainbow table = a big table of ready-made hashes to match.
290.why: A rainbow table holds precomputed password hashes. The attacker compares stolen hashes to the table to find the matching passwords fast.

291.tip: Flood a server with junk = DoS, Denial of Service.
291.why: A denial of service attack overwhelms a server with fake requests so real users can't get service. DNS poisoning changes records instead.

292.cue: known to the software vendor, but not patched
292.tip: Zero-day = zero days of patch protection.
292.why: A zero-day attack uses a flaw the vendor knows about or just learned of, before a patch is out. There are zero days of protection.

293.why: Zombies are infected computers in a botnet. Using many of them at once to flood a target is a distributed denial of service, DDoS.

294.why: Zombies are infected computers in a botnet. Using many of them at once to flood a target is a distributed denial of service, DDoS.

295.cue: table of words that potentially could be used as passwords
295.tip: List of words = dictionary attack. Precomputed hashes = rainbow table.
295.why: A dictionary attack tries each word from a word list as the password until one works.

296.why: DNS poisoning puts false records into a DNS server, so names point users to the wrong, often malicious, IP addresses.

297.cue: Touch ID or Face ID additional verification
297.tip: iPhone biometrics always have a backup: the passcode.
297.why: iOS requires you to set a passcode before using Touch ID or Face ID. It's the backup when your face or finger can't be read, and it's needed after a restart.

298.cue: prevented by creating a UEFI password
298.tip: UEFI password locks the UEFI settings, like boot order. It doesn't stop malware or phishing.
298.why: A UEFI password stops people from changing firmware settings. Without it someone could change the boot order and boot another OS to get around Windows security.

299.cue: monitor incoming and outgoing traffic and stop
299.tip: IPS = Intrusion Prevention System: it Prevents (stops) attacks. IDS only detects.
299.why: An intrusion prevention system watches traffic and blocks malicious activity in real time, not just reports it.

300.tip: Malware won't leave? Go to Safe Mode, where it can't run.
300.why: Safe Mode loads only the basic drivers and services, so most malware doesn't start and can then be removed.

301.tip: Mantrap = two doors, one person at a time. No tailgaters.
301.why: A mantrap is a small room with two doors where only one opens at a time, so a second person can't follow someone in.

302.tip: Redundancy of drives = RAID: Redundant Array of Independent Disks.
302.why: RAID stores data across several drives so that if one fails, the data is still safe on the others.

303.tip: Phishing tricks people, so train the people.
303.why: Phishing fools users into clicking or sharing data. Training teaches people to spot fake emails, which tech alone can't fully stop.

304.tip: No ports, no boot disk. Disable the USB and optical ports.
304.why: Disabling USB and other ports stops someone from plugging in a bootable disk to run hacking tools on the machine.

305.tip: Remote worker + private network = VPN, a secure tunnel.
305.why: A VPN makes an encrypted tunnel over the internet, so a traveling user can safely reach internal company resources.

306.tip: move = relocate (it leaves no copy behind). copy = keep both.
306.why: The move command takes a file out of one directory and puts it in another, so it no longer exists in the old place.

307.cue: Why would a gamer need to use the copy command
307.tip: copy = duplicate. The original stays where it is.
307.why: The copy command duplicates files to another location. Preparing a drive is format's job, and managing disks and partitions is diskpart's job.

308.tip: robocopy = Robust copy: copies groups of files reliably.
308.why: Robocopy, robust file copy, copies many files and folders from one place to another and can retry when copying fails.

309.tip: xcopy = extended copy: it brings subdirectories too.
309.why: xcopy copies files plus whole directory trees, including subdirectories. The plain copy command only copies files.

310.tip: format = prepare the drive with a file system.
310.why: format writes a file system to a drive or partition, so Windows can store files on it.

311.why: bootrec repairs boot records, such as the MBR and boot sector, when Windows won't start. sfc is the one for system files.

312.tip: ipconfig = IP configuration: shows your IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
312.why: ipconfig shows the IP settings of each network adapter, including its IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

313.tip: netstat = network statistics: lists active connections.
313.why: netstat shows active TCP connections and listening ports, which helps you see what the PC is talking to.

314.tip: nslookup = name server lookup: ask DNS.
314.why: nslookup sends queries to a DNS server to check how a name maps to an IP address, or the reverse.

315.tip: ping sends echo requests and waits for echo replies.
315.why: ping sends ICMP echo-request messages and listens for echo replies, a quick test of whether a destination is reachable.

316.tip: Local and wired: check the Cable and the Names (DNS). Gateway and ISP only matter beyond the LAN.
316.why: A bad cable breaks the wired link. If DNS fails, shares and printers found by name can't be reached. The gateway and ISP only matter for remote networks.

317.cue: authentication on behalf of all of the access points
317.tip: Many APs, one login server = RADIUS.
317.why: RADIUS is a central authentication server. All access points pass logins to it, which is secure and scales to many users.

318.tip: Old cartridges: Recycle by local rules, never the trash.
318.why: Ink cartridges contain chemicals, so they must be recycled or disposed of according to local regulations.

319.tip: ESD question? Pick the choice where you hold a bare component inside the case: CPU, RAM, motherboard.
319.why: Installing a CPU means touching a static-sensitive chip directly. A UPS or speakers are plugged in from outside and don't expose bare circuits.

320.why: DHCP servers listen on UDP port 67 for clients asking for an IP address.

321.why: Port 443 is used by HTTPS, the encrypted version of web traffic.

322.why: TFTP, Trivial File Transfer Protocol, uses UDP port 69.

323.why: Port 445 is used by SMB/CIFS, the protocol Windows uses to share files and printers.

324.why: Port 548 is used by AFP, Apple's file sharing protocol.

325.why: Port 80 is the standard port for unencrypted web traffic, HTTP.

326.why: TCP port 3389 is used by the Remote Desktop Protocol.

327.tip: gpUPDATE = UPDATE group policy now. gpresult = show the result.
327.why: gpupdate makes the PC refresh and apply the latest group policy settings right away, instead of waiting for the automatic refresh.

328.cue: Windows for file and printer sharing
328.tip: SMB = Share My Bits: Windows file and printer sharing.
328.why: SMB, Server Message Block, is the protocol Windows uses to share files and printers on a network. SMTP and IMAP are for email.

329.tip: VA = Very deep blacks: crystals tilt Vertically for high contrast.
329.why: VA panels tilt their liquid crystals vertically, which blocks light well and gives deep blacks and a high contrast ratio compared to TN and IPS.
