330.tip: GPT goes with UEFI and keeps a backup table. MBR goes with BIOS and has a 2 TB limit.
330.why: GPT is the partition style used with UEFI firmware, and it stores a backup copy of the partition table. The 2 TB limit and single table belong to MBR.

331.cue: reset option, retain the user's personal files
331.tip: Reset + Keep my files = Windows reinstalled, your files kept, your apps gone.
331.why: Reset this PC with Keep my files reinstalls Windows and keeps your personal files. Installed apps and settings are removed, so only user files come back.

keys.k: not a member of the administrator group

332.tip: Run as Administrator only works if you ARE an administrator.
332.why: Running something with elevated permission needs administrator rights. If the user isn't in the Administrators group, Windows won't grant them, so the action fails.

333.tip: Recovery USB = repair kit for when Windows won't start.
333.why: A recovery USB lets you start the PC and use repair tools when the installed Windows is too damaged to boot on its own.

334.cue: BIOS locates and reads the configuration settings

keys.k: first drive that contains a valid boot sector

334.tip: POST, CMOS settings, then boot the first drive with a valid boot sector.
334.why: After reading the CMOS settings, including the boot order, the BIOS boots from the first drive that has a valid boot sector.

335.tip: Kernel takes over -> NTOSKRNL starts WINLOGON -> then the Welcome screen.
335.why: After the kernel is in control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE. Displaying the Welcome screen is the step after that, so it's not next yet.

336.cue: Winload uses the path specified in BOOTMGR
336.tip: Path found, then load the core: NTOSKRNL and HAL.
336.why: Once Winload finds the boot partition, it loads the two core Windows files, the kernel NTOSKRNL.EXE and the hardware layer HAL.DLL.

337.cue: username and password are automatically populated
337.tip: Each browser keeps its own password store. Edge's saved logins don't show up in Chrome.
337.why: Saved passwords belong to the browser that saved them. Chrome does not save these login details automatically, so it doesn't fill them in the way Edge does.

338.tip: A library is a playlist for folders: it shows many folders in one place.
338.why: A Windows library gathers several folders from different locations into one view, without moving the files. It doesn't change file name length or encryption.

339.why: Multifactor authentication can use any number of factors, including three or more. 2FA is exactly two factors.

340.tip: Motherboard swap = lots of bare circuits. Ground yourself first.
340.why: Replacing a motherboard means handling a big board full of exposed chips. A static discharge from your body can damage them, so you use an antistatic wrist strap.

341.cue: six stages of the troubleshooting process
341.tip: I Eat Tacos, Eat Very Delicious: Identify, Establish theory, Test, Establish plan, Verify, Document.
341.why: You first identify the problem, guess a cause, and test it. Then you plan and apply the fix, verify everything works, and finally document what you did.

342.cue: Match the memory type to the feature
342.tip: DDR 184 pins. DDR2 240 pins at 1.8 V. DDR3 240 pins at 1.5 V. DDR4 288 pins. Newer = lower voltage.
342.why: Each DDR generation changed the module: DDR has 184 pins, DDR2 and DDR3 both have 240 pins but DDR3 uses less power (1.5 V vs 1.8 V), and DDR4 has 288 pins.

343.cue: Match the problem to the possible solution
343.tip: Swollen capacitors = new board. New CPU not fully seen = BIOS update. New video card, no video = plug in its power.
343.why: Bulging capacitors mean the board is failing. A BIOS update adds support for a new CPU. Big PCIe video cards need their own power cable. Fans with no beeps point to a bad cable or seated part.

344.cue: Windows 10 boot sequence after the boot manager
344.tip: W-N-R-K-W: Winload, NTOSKRNL and HAL, Registry and drivers, Kernel takes over, Winlogon.
344.why: Boot manager starts Winload, which loads the kernel and HAL, then reads the registry and drivers. The kernel then takes over and finally starts Winlogon for the sign-in.

345.tip: OpenGL = Open, cross-platform graphics. DirectX = Microsoft multimedia. Windows APIs = old apps work. Java APIs = Java coding.
345.why: OpenGL is an open graphics standard for any platform. DirectX is Microsoft's multimedia API set. Windows APIs keep older apps working, and Java APIs support Java development.

346.cue: tabs of the Windows 10 Task Manager
346.tip: Details = affinity. Performance = graphs. Startup = disable startup apps. Services = start or stop.
346.why: Details lets you set a process's CPU affinity. Performance shows resource use. Startup turns startup programs on or off. Services starts, stops and restarts services. Users is not used.

347.cue: drive status indicators in the Disk Management
347.tip: Healthy = volume OK. Online = disk OK. Initializing = going dynamic. Not Initialized = no signature. Offline = broken dynamic.
347.why: Healthy is a working volume and Online is a working disk. Initializing means a basic disk is being made dynamic. Not Initialized means no valid signature. Offline is a corrupted or missing dynamic disk.

348.tip: Personal = PSK password. Enterprise = RADIUS server. Open = nothing. WEP is not used.
348.why: WPA2-Personal uses AES with a shared password (PSK). WPA2-Enterprise sends logins to a RADIUS server. Open has no encryption or login.

349.tip: Scripts: VBScript, Python, JavaScript. Compiled: C++, C#, Java. JavaScript is not Java.
349.why: VBScript, Python and JavaScript are run by an interpreter line by line, so they are scripting languages. C++, C# and Java are compiled before they run.

350.tip: P-C-M-V: POST, CMOS, MBR, VBR, then bootmgr.
350.why: First POST tests the hardware, then the BIOS loads CMOS settings. Next it reads the MBR on the boot disk, which points to the VBR (volume boot record) that loads bootmgr.exe.

351.cue: Windows 10 version that best meets the described use
351.tip: Home = family. Education = schools. Pro = small business. Enterprise = big business.
351.why: Home is for personal use and family safety. Education is for schools with volume licensing. Pro adds business tools for small companies, and Enterprise adds advanced security and management for larger ones.

352.cue: file system with the respective description
352.tip: NTFS = huge and secure. exFAT = flash. FAT32 = 2 TB. CDFS = CDs. NFS = network.
352.why: NTFS supports 16 EB partitions and security. exFAT handles big files on flash drives. FAT32 partitions max at 2 TB. CDFS is for optical discs, and NFS shares files over a network.
